Keep this sheet open during the labs and the capstone. It covers the Week 7 concepts from Chapter 12, plus exposure assessment methods, which the textbook skips (marked \*).

## Key terms

| Term | Means |
|---|---|
| Pollution | A substance added to the environment faster than it can be dispersed, decomposed or diluted |
| Anthropocene | Proposed epoch in which human actions drive change in the Earth system |
| PM2.5 | Particles smaller than 2.5 microns that reach deep into the lungs |
| Point source | Pollution from one location, such as a discharge pipe |
| Nonpoint source | Diffuse pollution, such as farm and street runoff |
| Improved sanitation | Facilities that separate human waste from human contact |
| Open dump / controlled landfill / sanitary landfill | Disposal with little or no control / liner, compaction and daily cover / nearly all leachate contained and treated |
| Superfund | 1980 US law making polluters pay to clean up contaminated sites |
| Weather / climate | Short-term atmospheric conditions / long-term patterns |
| Mitigation / adaptation | Reducing greenhouse gases / reducing vulnerability to change |
| Environmental justice | Fair distribution of environmental hazards and fair enforcement of environmental law |

## Key numbers from the chapter

| Topic | Figure |
|---|---|
| Urban residents breathing air above WHO limits | Over 80%; 98% in low- and middle-income, 56% in high-income countries |
| Freeway exposure | Substantial within 300 ft; can extend past 1,000 ft |
| WHO annual PM2.5 guideline | 10 μg/m³ when the textbook was written; lowered to 5 μg/m³ in 2021\* |
| Wastewater discharged untreated | Over 80%; treated: about 70% (high-income) vs 8% (low-income) |
| People without improved sanitation | About 2.4 billion; about 1 billion practise open defecation |
| Municipal waste collected | About 98% (high-income) vs 41% (low-income) |
| Atmospheric CO₂ | Above 400 ppm by 2017 |
| Sea level rise since 1993 | About 80 mm |

Most at risk from climate change: drylands with variable rainfall, low-lying coasts with cyclones, and low atolls.

## Assessing exposure\*

| Method | Question it answers | ArcGIS Online tool |
|---|---|---|
| Proximity buffer | Who lives within a set distance of a source? | Create Buffers |
| Overlay | Which homes fall inside a hazard zone? | Overlay Layers |
| Interpolated surface | What is the value between monitors? | Interpolate Points |
| Summarize by area | How many people or homes are exposed in each tract? | Summarize Within |
| Community coverage | What share of neighbours have a protective factor? | Kernel or buffer around each home, then Summarize Within |

All analysis tools use credits. Test on a small area first.

## ArcGIS Online quick steps

Sign in at [emory.maps.arcgis.com](https://emory.maps.arcgis.com). Login instructions and free Esri training are on the [Emory GIS resources page](https://gis.ecds.emory.edu/). Esri renames menus from time to time, so if a label differs, look for the nearest match.

| To do this | Go to |
|---|---|
| Buffer a source | Analysis → Tools → Create Buffers; set distance (for example 300 ft) (uses credits) |
| Find homes inside a hazard area | Analysis → Tools → Overlay Layers, intersect homes with the hazard layer (uses credits) |
| Make a surface from monitors | Analysis → Tools → Interpolate Points, using monitor values (uses credits) |
| Count exposed people by area | Analysis → Tools → Summarize Within (uses credits) |
| Show exposure as a rate | Styles → choose the exposed count → Divided by → total population |

## Public health case: Tanser et al. 2018

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Households with piped water | 42% (2001) to 80% (2007) |
| Children tested | 2,105; 16.8% infected (boys 22.6%, girls 11.4%) |
| Local prevalence (kernel surface) | 0% to 85% |
| High-risk clusters | 4, around open water collection sites (relative risk 2.99–5.63) |
| Exposure measure | Share of households with piped water within 2 km of each child's home, averaged 2001–2007 |
| Adjusted odds of infection by coverage quintile (vs lowest) | Q2 0.39; Q3 0.30; Q4 0.16; Q5 0.12 |
| Each 1% increase in community coverage | About 2.5% lower odds of infection |
| Household piped water alone | Adjusted odds ratio 0.54 |

Main finding: community-level piped water coverage protected children far more than household access alone, because fewer neighbours using open water means less contamination for everyone.

## Critical lens

- **Environmental racism:** 1982 protests against a PCB landfill in majority-Black Warren County, North Carolina, helped launch the environmental justice movement. Hazardous facilities are often sited near communities of colour.
- **Global inequity:** wealthy countries have exported hazardous waste to poorer ones, prompting the Basel Convention (1989) and the African Bamako Convention (1991). Those least responsible for climate change are often most exposed.
- **Our study area:** piped water reached some communities years before others, and that sequence shows in children's infection risk.

## Capstone checklist

| Week | Show in your final map |
|---|---|
| 1 | Quality data with metadata; suitable projection; honest class breaks |
| 2 | Rates with the right denominator |
| 3 | Mobility or flows, where relevant |
| 4 | A joined table, a tested cluster, or a location quotient |
| 5 | Access: buffer or travel-time area |
| 6 | Two variables together, or a composite index |
| 7 | An exposure measure, plus a critical-lens note on whose data and whose history |

## Six questions to ask any exposure map

1. Measured, modelled or interpolated?
2. Household or community exposure?
3. Which distance, and why that distance?
4. Point or nonpoint source?
5. Crude or age-standardized outcomes?
6. Who lives next to the hazard, and why?

## Textbook corrections

- The chapter calls Hurricane Katrina "category 5". It was Category 3 at landfall.
- It places Syria in North Africa. Syria is in the Middle East.
